title: The drunken monkey
hookLine: a monkey, some wine, a scorpion, and the one watching the mind
carry: you are the watcher, not the monkey

cards: Start with a monkey. Restless already, the way monkeys are, never on one branch for long. Now somebody gives it wine to drink, and it gets wilder.
Then a scorpion stings it, and it leaps about in pain. And then, as if that weren't enough, a demon gets inside it. That's the creature Vivekananda asks his readers to look at in Raja Yoga.
He isn't talking about animals. He's describing the thing doing the reading.

teach.h: THE MONKEY IS RESTLESS BY NATURE.
teach.b: The picture comes in his chapter on pratyahara and dharana, drawing the mind in and holding it steady. He takes it piece by piece. The mind is restless by nature, like the monkey.

teach.h: WINE, SCORPION, DEMON: DESIRE, JEALOUSY, PRIDE.
teach.b: Then desire gets into it: that is the wine. Jealousy at someone else's good fortune stings it: the scorpion. Last comes pride, the demon, and now it thinks nothing in the world matters but itself.
You might expect a scolding next.

teach.h: FIRST LESSON: LET IT RUN, AND WATCH.
teach.b: Instead comes a gentle first lesson. Sit for a while, he says, and let the mind run on. Don't fight it.
Just watch it. Some of the thoughts, he warns, may astonish you. Keep watching anyway.
With practice, he says, the jumping slowly lessens. Underneath that advice sits one of the big ideas of Hindu yoga. In the Yoga Sutras, the mind belongs to what is seen, part of nature, prakriti.

teach.h: THE SEER IS NOT THE MONKEY.
teach.b: You, the one who sees, are something else: the purusha, the seer. Vedanta has its own word for it, the sakshi, the witness. So the monkey is real, but it isn't you.
That's why watching comes first. Until the watching starts, the mind simply is the monkey, swinging from a worry to a text message to an old argument, and calling it thinking.
The moment a jump is noticed, there's a little gap. The one watching and the jump are not the same thing. That gap is where Raja Yoga begins.

how: Students of Vivekananda's Raja Yoga often begin with short daily sits in which they let the mind wander and simply observe it, before moving on to concentration practices; the book is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers.

o: a plan for winning arguments about the mind
a way of keeping the mind busy every minute
a yoga of the mind that begins by watching it

games.q: the monkey, piece by piece — tap the pairs.

s: Vivekananda's first lesson is to force the mind to stop thinking
his first lesson is the opposite: let the mind run on, and watch it.
in the Yoga tradition, the seer and the mind it watches are not the same
the mind is part of nature, prakriti; the seer is the purusha. Vedanta calls the watcher the sakshi, the witness.
in the picture, the monkey stands for an animal we should avoid
the monkey is the mind: restless, then drunk with desire, stung by jealousy, possessed by pride.

games.q: you sit and watch your mind jump, and you notice: i'm seeing this. what does Hindu yoga say that noticing points to?
o: nothing more: the mind is all you are.
the seer, which watches the mind and isn't the mind.
a second, smaller monkey that needs calming too.
games.why: in the Yoga Sutras the mind is part of what is seen. the one who sees, the purusha, is something else. watching the monkey is the first taste of that.

practice: Try the first lesson exactly as it's given: don't try to calm anything, let the mind run, and when a thought jumps up, a plan, a memory, a complaint, just notice it, the way you'd watch a monkey move between branches from a park bench.
No chasing it, no shooing it away, and if a thought comes that you'd rather not have, let it be seen too. If you pray, you can hold the watching itself as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's yoga of the mind, which begins by watching the mind jump, from the seat of the one who sees.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: raja yoga, the name Vivekananda gives the yoga of the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: you are the watcher, not the monkey. Tomorrow, another of his pictures: a lake, and what lives at the bottom of it. Day nine hundred forty-seven, and counting.

sources.ref: Raja Yoga, the chapter 'Pratyahara and Dharana' (the monkey, and the first lesson of watching the mind)
Yoga Sutras 2.17–2.21 (the seer and the seen)
